title: Choosing Alternatives with switch
learningObjectives: Explain the key idea in choosing alternatives with switch.
Identify the relevant syntax and rules.
Trace each example and predict the result.
Apply the concept in a small program.
Avoid a common mistake related to this topic.

understand.concept: A switch statement selects among cases based on an integral, enumeration or compatible constant expression value. Each case typically ends with break to prevent unintended fall-through. A default branch handles unmatched values.
understand.whyItMatters: switch can make menu choices and discrete-value logic clearer than long chains of equality checks.
understand.analogy: Think of this as a control or calculation rule that tells a program how to handle a particular situation consistently.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is only a starting point; C++ syntax, types and execution rules determine actual behaviour.
understand.explain:
## Case labels
Each case label names a value to match. Case values must be compile-time constants and cannot duplicate within a switch.

## break and default
`break` exits the switch. `default` handles values with no matching case and is optional.

## Fall-through
If a case does not break, execution may continue into later case statements. Modern C++ also provides `[[fallthrough]]` to document intentional fall-through.

examples.title: Simple menu
examples.code: int choice{2};\nswitch (choice) { case 1: std::cout << "Start"; break; case 2: std::cout << "Help"; break; default: std::cout << "Unknown"; }

examples.title: Default branch
examples.code: int option{9};\nswitch (option) { case 1: std::cout << "One"; break; default: std::cout << "Other"; }

examples.title: Break prevents fall-through
examples.code: int day{1};\nswitch (day) { case 1: std::cout << "Mon"; break; case 2: std::cout << "Tue"; break; }
examples.explanation: The break exits after the selected case.

examples.title: Multiple labels
examples.code: char grade{'A'};\nswitch (grade) { case 'A': case 'B': std::cout << "Pass"; break; default: std::cout << "Review"; }
examples.explanation: A and B share the same action.

examples.title: Enum choice
examples.code: enum class Mode { Read, Write };\nMode mode{Mode::Read};\nswitch (mode) { case Mode::Read: std::cout << "Read"; break; case Mode::Write: std::cout << "Write"; break; }

practise.guidedTask: Choose one example from this lesson. Predict its result before running it, change one input or condition, predict again, then explain the difference. Compile and test locally if a C++ compiler is available.
practise.independentTask: Write a small C++ program that demonstrates choosing alternatives with switch in a meaningful scenario. Include at least two test cases and explain how the code behaves at boundaries or unexpected inputs.
